# Demonstration of Measurement-Enhanced State Preparation and Erasure Conversion in a Molecular Tweezer Array

Connor M. Holland ,1 Yukai Lu ,1,2 Samuel J. Li ,1

Callum L. Welsh ,1 and Lawrence W. Cheuk 1,*

1Department of Physics, Princeton University, Princeton, New Jersey 08544, USA 2Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Princeton University, Princeton, New Jersey 08544, USA

(Received 18 June 2024; accepted 17 June 2025; published 16 July 2025)

Programmable optical tweezer arrays of molecules are an emerging platform for quantum simulation and quantum information science. For these applications, the reduction and mitigation of errors remain major challenges. In this work, we leverage the rich internal structure of molecules to mitigate two types of errors —internal state preparation and qubit leakage errors. First, we demonstrate robust measurement-enhanced tweezer preparation at a record fidelity using site-resolved error detection followed by tweezer movement. Second, using a new hyperfine qubit encoding well suited for use as a quantum memory, we demonstrate site-resolved detection of qubit leakage errors (erasures) induced by blackbody radiation. This approach constitutes the first demonstration of erasure conversion in molecules, a capability that has found recent interest in quantum error correction. Our work opens the door to new possibilities with molecular tweezer arrays: Measurement-enhanced preparation opens access to mesoscopic defect-free molecular arrays that are important for quantum simulation of interacting many-body systems; erasure conversion in molecular arrays lays the technical groundwork for midcircuit detection, an important capability for explorations in quantum information processing.

I. INTRODUCTION

Programmable optical tweezer arrays of ultracold molecules are an emerging platform for quantum science [1]. They combine the microscopic detection and control capabilities offered by programmable optical tweezer arrays [2,3] with the richness of molecules such as their complex internal structures and long-ranged and anisotropic interactions [4–6]. These features enable applications in many areas ranging from quantum information processing [7–9] and quantum simulation of novel many-body Hamiltonians [1,10–13] to precision measurement experiments probing fundamental physics beyond the Standard Model [11,13–16]. Starting with the first demonstrations of trapping and high-fidelity detection of single molecules in optical tweezer traps [17–21], recent work has demonstrated highly coherent rotational qubits [6,22,23], observed coherent dipolar interactions between individually held

molecules, and demonstrated on-demand entanglement and two-qubit gates between rotational molecular qubits [24–27]. These works established the building blocks for quantum information processing and quantum simulation with molecular tweezer arrays. A major experimental challenge for molecular tweezer arrays—and for any quantum platform—is mitigation of errors that occur during the preparation and subsequent evolution of the quantum system. In addition to reducing sources of these errors, a powerful and complementary approach is to mitigate errors via detection and subsequent postselection or feedback. In particular, for programmable optical tweezer arrays of atoms and molecules, siteresolved detection of errors, in some cases, allows their subsequent removal simply through tweezer rearrangement. In previous work with atomic tweezer arrays, siteresolved detection has been used to increase internal state preparation fidelities [28], increase robustness to radiative decays of Rydberg states [28,29], and lower motional temperatures [30]. In recent work with bialkali molecules, site-resolved error detection was used to enhance molecular formation efficiencies and reduce array defect rates [31,32]. In addition to mitigating these classical errors, site-resolved detection of qubit errors with known locations, so-called quantum erasures [33,34], is also useful. In particular, recent work has shown that conversion of qubit errors into

In this paper, we demonstrate new schemes to mitigate two types of errors in molecular tweezer arrays: state preparation errors and qubit leakage errors. Our general strategy is to leverage the rich internal structure of molecules and site-resolved imaging for local error detection midsequence. Specifically, we encode errors into a set of “bright” internal states whose optical detection minimally affects error-free molecules residing in “dark” internal states. To mitigate state preparation errors, we demonstrate a robust scheme that detects internal state errors locally and subsequently corrects them via tweezer rearrangement. This process allows us to achieve tweezer preparation fidelities substantially surpassing previous work [24,43]. Crucially, the fidelities achieved allow immediate access to defect-free mesoscopic arrays and open the door to quantum simulation in the many-body regime with molecular arrays. To mitigate qubit leakage errors, we demonstrate a new scheme that detects qubit leakages midsequence for a new noninteracting qubit encoding suitable for use as a quantum memory. We encode errors in states that can be detected locally while minimally affecting qubit population and coherence, and we show that a significant source of errors arising from absorption of blackbody radiation can be converted into locally detectable errors, i.e., erasures. We show that excision of erasures significantly improves qubit lifetimes and coherence times, constituting the first demonstration of erasure conversion in molecules. Our erasure conversion work adds an important capability to the molecular quantum information processing toolkit. It lays the groundwork for midcircuit measurement and quantum error correction in molecular tweezer arrays.

II. OUR PLATFORM: PROGRAMMABLE OPTICAL TWEEZER ARRAYS OF LASER-COOLED MOLECULES

Our experiment uses laser-cooled CaF molecules trapped in a programmable optical tweezer array. A CaF molecular beam is created using a cryogenic buffer gas cell [44], laser slowed [45], and trapped in a magneto-optical trap (MOT) [46,47]. Subsequently, the molecules are laser cooled to sub-Doppler temperatures [48,49], optically trapped [50], and transferred into a rearrangeable 1D array of optical tweezer traps [17,19]. Because of the light-assisted collisions, each tweezer is either empty or holds one molecule. The loading process is stochastic, with a typical loading probability of 20% to 30%. Molecules in the X2Σðv ¼ 0; N ¼ 1Þ rovibrational manifold [where v (N) denote the vibrational (rotational) quantum number] can be cooled and optically detected

using the X2Σðv¼0;N ¼1Þ→A2Π1=2ðv¼0;J¼1=2;þÞ closed optical cycling transition [Fig. 1(a)]. Consequently, molecules occupy all twelve hyperfine states of X2Σðv ¼ 0; N ¼ 1Þ following tweezer loading. To determine each tweezer’s occupation, we apply laser-cooling light on the same cycling transition and collect the emitted fluorescence onto an EMCCD camera. This protocol detects molecules in all X2Σðv ¼ 0; N ¼ 1Þ hyperfine states [Fig. 1(a)].

To this end, we make use of the rich set of available internal molecular states. We encode errors into a set of bright states (F) that can be optically detected while keeping error-free

Specifically, we make use of bright and dark states whose optical transitions are well separated compared to their linewidths. This strategy is generally possible in a quantum system with sufficiently rich internal structure. For example, work in alkaline-earth atomic arrays [28–30,35] has used ground and metastable electronic manifolds with widely separated optical transitions. Instead of two different electronic manifolds, our strategy makes use of two different rotational manifolds. The rotational manifold F ¼ X2Σðv ¼ 0; N ¼ 1Þ, which permits optical cycling, is used to flag errors, while error-free molecules reside in the ground rovibrational manifold T ¼ X2Σðv ¼ 0; N ¼ 0Þ [Fig. 1(a)]. The optical transitions of the bright states in F are separated from those in the dark states T by Δ ≈2π × 20 GHz, which is much larger than the excited state linewidth of Γ ≈2π × 10 MHz. Optical detection of errors encoded as population in F should therefore minimally affect population and coherence in T .

IV. NEW SITE-RESOLVED IMAGING SCHEME TO DETECT ERRORS

Experimentally, we first show that molecules in the bright statesF canindeed bedetected whileminimallyaffectingthe population of error-free molecules residing in the dark states T . To this end, we devise a new fluorescence detection scheme that is optimized for minimally affecting the dark states. This method is in contrast to previous imaging schemes that prioritize detection fidelity [17,19,48]. In our scheme, we seek to minimize exposure to imaging light in order to minimize off-resonant scattering by errorfree molecules in dark states. At the same time, high photon scattering rates of the bright states improve the signal-tonoise ratio of fluorescence detection. We therefore use light resonant with the X2Σðv ¼ 0; N ¼ 1Þ →A2Π1=2ðv ¼ 0; J ¼ 1=2; þÞ transition. This approach provides the best ratio of fluorescence emission to off-resonant scattering and also enables rapid detection compared to previous imaging schemes using detuned laser-cooling light [17,19,48]. We quantify the performance of our detection scheme using two metrics: (1) the classification fidelity and (2) the effect on error-free dark states. To classify a tweezer site as having occupation in F, i.e., having an error, we binarize the fluorescence counts with a threshold θE;0. Sites with counts above θE;0 are classified as errors; those below θE;0 are classified as error-free. The classification fidelity is determined by the false-negative probability ϵ10, where a site with an error is classified as error-free, and the falsepositive probability ϵ01, where an error-free site is classified as having an error. Both misclassification probabilities depend on θE;0. Here, we prioritize minimizing ϵ10 rather than the overall fidelity because, for error mitigation via postselection, ϵ01 only affects the data rate while ϵ10 directly affects the ability to reject errors. After optimization, we find that, at an imaging intensity of

I ¼ 4.5 mW=cm2, an imaging duration of 3 ms, and a tweezer depth of kB × 930ð20Þ μK, we achieve a falsenegative probability ϵ10ðθE;0Þ ¼ 0.033ð4Þ at a threshold of θE ¼ θE;0 ¼ 4.8 [Fig. 1(b)]. This imaging performance allows up to a 30-fold reduction of intrinsic error rates. Next, we quantify the effect of our imaging procedure on the dark state population. We prepare molecules in one of the dark states j−i ¼ jX2Σðv ¼ 0; N ¼ 0Þ; J ¼ 1=2; F ¼ 1; mF ¼ −1i and measure the population loss versus imaging duration [Fig. 1(c)]. At the imaging duration used (3 ms), we measure a population loss of 3.8ð3Þ × 10−3 per image, confirming that the error-free states are minimally affected. The population loss rate is in agreement with theoretical estimates. For our scheme, the ratio of the offresonant scattering rate to the fluorescence rate is approximately 9Γ2=Δ2 ∼10−6 (Appendix E). Because the dark states do not optically cycle, they leak to other internal states after Oð1Þ scattering events. Since we typically scatter about 1000 photons to achieve a sufficient signalto-noise ratio, the population leakage errors are expected to be at about the 10−3 level. These leakage errors could, in principle, be corrected with more elaborate optical pumping and detection schemes.

V. ROBUST AND ENHANCED TWEEZER PREPARATION USING SITE-RESOLVED ERROR DETECTION

Having established that bright molecules in F can be detected without affecting dark ones in T , we next demonstrate how this finding can be used to detect and correct for internal state preparation errors. In previous work with laser-cooled molecular arrays, the best reported fidelity of having a tweezer loaded with a molecule in a single internal state was approximately 80%, limited by imperfect optical pumping and microwave transfers [24,25]. Here, we present a scheme that detects internal state preparation errors, allowing them to be subsequently removed either midsequence or through postselection. Our scheme, shown in Fig. 2(a), works as follows. After initial tweezer loading, molecules are optically pumped into a single hyperfine state jD0i ¼ jX2Σðv ¼ 0; N ¼ 1Þ; J ¼ 3=2; F ¼ 2; mF ¼ −2i within F. Subsequently, molecules are state-selectively shelved into one of the dark states j−i with a microwave pulse at approximately 20.5 GHz. All errors due to imperfect optical pumping and microwave transfer leave a molecule in the bright states F, which is then optically detected with our resonant imaging scheme without substantially affecting the correctly prepared molecules that reside in the dark state j−i. We quantify the performance of our measurementenhanced state preparation scheme as follows. We first perform internal state preparation followed by error detection, which provides a list of sites that are flagged as having an error. Subsequently, we transfer correctly prepared

Thus, future work that reduces these losses could allow substantial improvement. Lastly, our scheme enables midsequence removal of preparation errors via tweezer rearrangement. We first create regularly spaced defect-free arrays of molecules in F and nondestructively detect their occupation [24]. Subsequently, we apply our measurement-enhanced state preparation protocol. While previous experiments with atomic arrays have incorporated similar techniques to postselect for no errors [28], to our knowledge, our work is the first demonstration of midsequence removal of internal state preparation errors. This capability will be crucial for quantum simulation and computation applications that require large-scale arrays at low defect rates. Already, our measurement-enhanced preparation scheme opens the door to quantum simulation of interacting many-body Hamiltonians in defect-free mesoscopic molecular arrays. We achieve an overall fidelity of 60(4)% for arrays of size n ¼ 10, which makes practical postselection for perfect arrays possible with only a modest data rate reduction of around 40%.

VI. DETECTING QUBIT LEAKAGE ERRORS

The second part of our work concerns detecting qubit leakage errors. First, we demonstrate a new qubit encoding using two noninteracting hyperfine states in the dark state manifold T . Second, we devise a scheme (“erasure imaging”) to optically detect population in the bright states F while minimally affecting both population and coherence of the dark qubit. Lastly, we show that a significant source of error for the new qubit—leakage into other molecular states induced by blackbody radiation—can be converted to population in bright states, which can be detected as local errors. These local qubit errors are known as erasures [33,34], a topic that has attracted much attention in both theoretical [35–38] and experimental work in

A. New hyperfine qubit in CaF

In previous work using CaF molecules, coherent interactions and two-qubit gates were demonstrated using a rotational qubit encoding [24,25]. Specifically, two interacting states from two neighboring rotational manifolds, j↑i ¼ jX2Σðv ¼ 0; N ¼ 1Þ; J ¼ 1=2; F ¼ 0; mF ¼ 0i and j↓i ¼ jX2Σðv ¼ 0; N ¼ 0Þ; J ¼ 1=2; F ¼ 1;mF ¼ 0i, were used. Here, we utilize a new noninteracting qubit encoding suitable for storing quantum information. Specifically, our encoding uses the two hyperfine states j1i ¼ jX2Σðv ¼ 0; N ¼ 0Þ; J ¼ 1=2; F ¼ 1; mF ¼ 0i and j0i ¼ jX2Σðv ¼ 0; N ¼ 0Þ; J ¼ 1=2; F ¼ 0; mF ¼ 0i, both from the ground rovibrational manifold X2Σðv ¼ 0; N ¼ 0Þ [Fig. 3(a)]. These states are predicted to have long coherence times because of the absence of tensor ac Stark shifts and their low magnetic moments. In addition, they are naturally compatible with our error mitigation scheme, as they belong to the dark state manifold T . We note that hyperfine qubit encodings in molecules have been previously proposed for use in quantum information processing [8], and hyperfine coherence times have been measured previously in the bialkali molecules NaK [52], RbCs [53], and NaRb [54]. Very recent work concurrent with ours has also demonstrated a hyperfine qubit encoding in bialkali NaCs molecules trapped in an optical tweezer array [27]. We first demonstrate coherent control over this new hyperfine qubit and show that it has long coherence times. We coherently control the qubit by driving an M1 transition (at approximately 122 MHz) through a two-photon Raman process. Specifically, we use light detuned halfway between the X −A2Π1=2 and X −A2Π3=2 transitions (single-photon detuning of ΔXA ≈2π × 1.1 THz) [Fig. 3(b)]. The two frequencies in the Raman light copropagate and have σþ projections. To demonstrate coherent control, we prepare molecules in j1i and apply Raman light for a variable duration. As shown in Fig. 3(c), we observe Rabi oscillations at ΩR ≈2π × 15 kHz. We next measure the qubit coherence time using a Ramsey sequence consisting of two Raman π=2 pulses separated by a variable duration. To minimize inhomogeneous light shifts between sites due to tweezer trapping light, we operate at a tweezer depth of Uhf ¼ kB × 39ð1Þ μK. By measuring the decay rate of the amplitude of the Ramsey fringe, we find a bare coherence time of T 2 ¼ 19.5ð7Þ ms, which can be increased to T2 ¼ 288ð15Þ ms with a single spin echo. We further extend the coherence time to 1710(60) ms by applying dynamical decoupling with an XY8 pulse sequence (pulse separation of 33.3 ms) [Fig. 3(d)]. In addition to having long coherence times, this hyperfine qubit can be interfaced with the rotational qubit used in

previous work [22,24,25]. Specifically, we have verified that a quantum state can be coherently transferred from the rotational encoding (j↑i; j↓i) to the hyperfine encoding (j1i; j0i) (Appendix I).

We base our new detection scheme off of the rapid imaging procedure described in Sec. IV. C. Erasure conversion and detection of qubit leakage errors induced by blackbody radiation

Having quantified the performance of our composite erasure imaging scheme, we next use it to mitigate a significant error for our hyperfine qubit—leakage into higher vibrational states due to blackbody radiation at room temperature. Specifically, blackbody radiation drives Δv ¼ 1 vibrational-changing E1 transitions, leading to leakage from the qubit states (encoded in v ¼ 0) to the vibrationally excited states E ¼ X2Σðv ¼ 1; N ¼ 1Þ. The estimated leakage rate is Γ01 ≈0.3 s−1 [56], which is a slow but significant source of qubit loss. As we will show, these errors can be converted to population in the bright states F and detected in a site-resolved manner. In other words, the leakage errors can be converted into erasures and detected. To perform erasure conversion, we simply apply v ¼ 1 vibrational repumping light that repumps molecules into the bright manifold F with 98% probability [Fig. 5(a)]. There are, however, two subtleties. First, vibrationally excited molecules in X2Σðv ¼ 1Þ decay back to the ground vibrational manifold X2Σðv ¼ 0Þ at a rate Γ10 ≈5.3 s−1, which is much quicker than the blackbody excitation rate Γ01 ≈0.3 s−1. Therefore, erasure conversion should occur at a rate much faster than Γ10. It is not necessary, however, to detect the error flags in F quickly since they lie in the long-lived ground vibrational manifold. Second, blackbody radiation causes secondary leakage of molecules out of the detectable bright states F into the undetected dark states X2Σðv ¼ 1; N ¼ 0; 2Þ [Fig. 5(b)]. These states then decay both back to F and also to another dark rotational manifold X2Σðv ¼ 0; N ¼ 3Þ. We close this leakage pathway by applying rotational repumping light (N ¼ 3 repumper) that brings X2Σðv ¼ 0; N ¼ 3Þ molecules back to the error flag manifold F [Fig. 5(b)].

We first experimentally confirm that secondary blackbody leakage is indeed suppressed by N ¼ 3 repumping light. We indeed find that with the extra repumping light, the error flags F have a population lifetime of τ ¼ 13.5ð5Þ s, well exceeding the blackbody-limited lifetime by a factor of approximately 4. The residual loss is attributed to background gas collisions and double blackbody excitation events into dark rotational manifolds with N ≥5 (Appendix J). We next experimentally implement our blackbody erasure conversion scheme and investigate whether it extends qubit population lifetimes and coherence times. We measure the offset and amplitude of Ramsey fringes with and without erasure excision. For these measurements, erasure conversion is repeatedly applied midcircuit, with erasure detection occurring once at the end of the sequence. VII. DISCUSSION AND OUTLOOK

In summary, we have demonstrated two error mitigation schemes for state preparation errors and qubit leakage errors. Specifically, we demonstrated (1) a measurementenhanced state preparation scheme that enables robust and record-level fidelities for preparing defect-free and internally pure molecular arrays, and (2) an erasure conversion and detection scheme for blackbody-induced leakage errors of a hyperfine qubit. Both parts of our work represent key new capabilities in the quantum control of molecules. Our measurement-enhanced state preparation work is the first demonstration of removal of internal state errors following midsequence error detection; our erasure conversion work constitutes the first demonstration of erasure conversion in molecules. Our error mitigation work opens several possibilities. First, state preparation fidelities of approximately 95% open the door to quantum simulation of many-body Hamiltonians with low defect rates. In particular, for mesoscopic systems of Oð10Þ particles, we can postselect on perfectly prepared arrays with a tolerable level of data reduction. Second, our work lays the foundations for exploring erasure conversion in the context of quantum error correction with molecular qubits. For quantum error correction, erasure conversion is useful when the dominant errors— often from two-qubit gates—are converted and detected [35]. Our current work concerns erasure conversion of a significant source of leakage errors in noninteracting hyperfine qubits.
